# Puṇṇovāda Sutta (MN 145 (PTS MN iii 267))

**ID:** MN 145 (PTS MN iii 267)

**Title (English, from literature):** Advice to Puṇṇa

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Puṇṇovāda Sutta* ("Advice to Puṇṇa", MN 145; PTS MN iii 267) is the 145th discourse of the Majjhimanikāya [SuttaCentral]. It recounts the exchange between the Buddha and the monk Puṇṇa (Sanskrit: Pūrṇa), who wishes to depart for Sunāparanta (Śroṇāparāntaka) to practice and propagate the Dhamma [SuttaCentral; Baruah 2000; Bodhi 2003]. Warning him that the people of Sunāparanta are fierce and violent, the Buddha questions Puṇṇa on how he will react if they verbally abuse, physically assault, or even kill him [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Anālayo]. Puṇṇa responds with steadfast equanimity, reflecting at each escalating threat that his assailants are kind for not subjecting him to worse violence [Anālayo]. The discourse also records the Buddha's guidance regarding the cessation of delight (*nandī*) in sensory objects [Shulman 2014], and the Buddha praises Puṇṇa for practicing in accordance with the Dhamma without troubling him over matters of interpretation [Flores 2008].

MN 145 opens the "Decade on the Six Sense-bases" (MN 145–152), a group of discourses distinguished by their lack of parallels in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* and their close correspondence to the *Ṣaḍāyatana-saṃyukta* of the *Saṃyuktāgama* [Dhammadinna 2014]. SuttaCentral and modern scholarship identify full parallels in the Pali canon at SN 35.88 (*Puṇṇasutta*), the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 311 in T 99), an individual Chinese translation (T 108), the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya (T 1448.3), the Sanskrit *Divyāvadāna* (chapter 2, *Pūrṇāvadāna*), and the Tibetan Kangyur (D 1) [SuttaCentral; Dhammadinna 2014; Tatelman 1988]. DharmaNexus confirms substantial Pali-internal text reuse with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35, where §3.8–8.5 matches §88.2.6–88.20.2 with 0.94 similarity) and computes close alignments with the Sanskrit *Divyāvadāna* and *Avadānaśataka*, as well as Chinese translations T 108 and T 99 [DharmaNexus]. The commentary (*Puṇṇovādasuttavaṇṇanā*) elaborates Puṇṇa's background as a merchant from Śūrpāraka and became an influential textual source for regional narratives, including Burmese chronicles [Pranke] and Siamese literature combining the sutta and commentary into footprint pilgrimage lore [Lamotte 1988; Skilling].
